A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReSA and Answer-Then-Check research. The main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching experiments and examples moved or renumbered in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning experiments, jailbreak-defense and general-capability scores, safe-completion evaluations, efficiency measurements and ablations in Sections 4-5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds RL, adaptive checking, additional attack evaluations, summary-safety measurements and failure analyses, particularly in Appendices G-I.

M1.justification: v2 retains the original SFT method but introduces adaptive bypass of safety reasoning for ordinary queries and GRPO-based ReSA-RL. The latter rewards intended-summary safety, final-answer safety, benign-query compliance and output format. These additions materially change training objectives and inference behavior (Sections 3.5-3.6).

E1.justification: The original safety and capability benchmarks remain. v2 adds ordinary instruction-tuning examples from Tulu-3 and extends evaluation to white-box GCG, AutoDAN-Turbo and prompts containing prefilled safety-check sequences. In particular, gradient-access attacks and prefilling broaden the tested threat conditions beyond v1's evaluation.

E2.justification: The established defense comparators are retained. v2 adds an evaluated post-hoc gpt-oss-safeguard-20b comparator alongside LlamaGuard, the base model and ReSA-SFT in Table 17, constituting a limited extension of the baseline set.

E3.justification: Alongside retained SFT settings, v2 introduces GRPO training with 10 epochs, batch size 512 and eight rollouts per prompt, plus a Gemma-3-4b-it configuration. New attack protocols include GCG on 50 prompts and AutoDAN-Turbo on 100 prompts with a fixed learned strategy library. Separate summary-safety evaluation and runtime measurements also expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: The original training-size and WJ-only ablations are retained. v2 adds robustness tests for GCG, AutoDAN-Turbo and prefilling; analyses of adaptive checking's efficiency and capability tradeoffs; intended-summary safety tests; and measurements of safety-check failures. Appendix I also adds evaluator-error and STAIR-DPO comparison case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new GRPO rollout count specifies training sampling, not repeated evaluation or uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Original principal safety scores and WJ-only ablation results are retained after reorganization. v2 adds extensive RL, adaptive, Gemma, attack, runtime and summary-safety results; Table 2 adds Llama ReSA-RL at 0.9932 average LlamaGuard DSR alongside unchanged ReSA-SFT at 0.9046. A retained value also changes incorrectly: the Llama base over-refusal average becomes 93.27% rather than 92.60%, despite unchanged component scores.

T1.justification: Section 3.6 newly defines sequential rollout variables and a piecewise reward for harmful, benign and normal queries. This is a limited addition of mathematical definitions accompanying RL, without new theorems or proofs. Algorithm 1 primarily restates the existing dataset-curation procedure.

C1.justification: v2 adds adaptive efficiency and RL-based summary safety as contributions in the introduction and conclusion, and explicitly claims in the abstract that inference-time strategies alone are insufficient. The original claims about the 80K dataset, safety versus over-refusal tradeoff, safe completion and effectiveness with 500 examples remain.

C2.justification: v1 treats making internal summaries safe through RL as future work; v2 interprets its RL results as supporting disclosure of reasoning and claims elimination of the exposure risk. New discussions attribute some failures to evaluator bias or ambiguity, assess safety-check reliability and explain inference-time defenses' limitations through insufficient safety-policy knowledge.

D1.justification: v2 adds RL reward coefficients, framework and training settings, attack budgets and prefilling text, safeguard prompts, runtime hardware information and an explicit over-refusal judge. It also supplies dataset-curation pseudocode and directly reports a public ReSA dataset location in the abstract and Appendix B. Existing curation and baseline templates largely remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting its extensions, including Tulu-3, DeepSeekMath/GRPO, HybridFlow, Gemma 3, AutoDAN-Turbo, SafeChain and gpt-oss-safeguard. Related work gives STAIR-DPO and Realsafe-r1 more explicit discussion, while retaining the central distinction from Deliberative Alignment.

P1.justification: v2 extensively condenses and rewrites existing method, experimental-setup, results and discussion prose. It reorganizes implementation details and case studies into Appendices F and J, separates full results and additional discussions into G and I, and restructures the narrative around the original method and its variants.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 2 are redrawn. The original safety tables are reorganized by benchmark into v2 Tables 2, 7 and 8, while the original over-refusal and reasoning tables are merged into Table 3. Numerous new experimental tables and case panels are added, and retained examples gain clearer highlighting of user-visible output.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves safer internal summaries to future RL work and assesses efficiency through token length. v2 implements and evaluates RL and adaptive variants, separately tests summary safety, measures runtime and broadens threat testing, substantially strengthening evidence about practical risks and costs. Added settings and dataset-access information improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh localized problems: lower Llama reasoning accuracy under RL, the inconsistent baseline average in Table 3, and assurances of harmless reasoning exposure that exceed Table 16's benchmark evidence.
